the_window_is_the_units_own_start_and_a_.description: THE TRAP THE ORDER NAMES, and the one that matters most on this read: the count must cover the whole life of the running unit. A relative window (--since '-40 min', say) would begin AFTER the unit started and a capture in the gap would be invisible -- and this baseline is what authorises a first sign-in, so a false zero here is the costly direction. A second hazard sits behind it: systemd prints ActiveEnterTimestamp as 'Sun 2026-10-11 16:09:55 UTC', which journalctl --since does not take verbatim, so it must be normalised, and a silently failed normalisation would hand journalctl an empty --since.
the_window_is_the_units_own_start_and_a_.expected_landed: the window is derived from the unit's own ActiveEnterTimestamp, the raw stamp is printed so a reader can re-derive it, and a failed conversion prints SIGNIN_WINDOW_UNRESOLVED and NO SIGNIN_LINES line at all
the_window_is_the_units_own_start_and_a_.expected_not_landed: a relative window, or an empty --since, or a count printed beside an unresolved window -- any of which would produce a number whose scope in TIME is narrower than the sentence beside it
the_window_is_the_units_own_start_and_a_.observed: START=Sun 2026-10-11 16:09:55 UTC is printed, and it EQUALS the ActiveEnterTimestamp st32's own V1 read printed at install time, so the window covers the unit's whole life on this root. The count was taken with --since on the normalised form of that exact stamp. SIGNIN_WINDOW_UNRESOLVED occurrences: 0, so the conversion succeeded; and because the SIGNIN_LINES line lives in the ELSE branch of that check, AC2's presence test would have failed rather than passing on a bad window. RESTARTS=0 corroborates that the unit has not restarted since, so there is no earlier start whose window this read would miss.
